title: Unilateral Reduction of Employees' Salaries in the Context of COVID-19 Pandemic: Macsteel Service Centres SA (Pty) Ltd v National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (NUMSA) 2020 8 BLLR 772 (LC)
author: Chillion H Ncube
summary: In Macsteel Service Centres SA (Pty) Ltd v National Union of Metal Workers of South Africa (NUMSA) 2020 8 BLLR 772 (LC), the Labour Court handed down a judgment relating to a salary cut imposed by an employer due to COVID-19 and lockdown. The case came before the Labour Court as an urgent application by Macsteel ("employer") to interdict an unprotected strike by NUMSA. The judgment specifically dealt with the issue as to whether a unilateral reduction of salaries imposed by the employer for the months of May, June and July 2020 was unlawful as contemplated in sections 64(4) and (5) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995. The Labour Court made a detailed analysis of Macsteel's operations and concluded that where employees had tendered services, they are entitled to full remuneration. The court found that the 20% salary reduction was unlawful as it amounted to a unilateral change to employees' conditions of employment. The Macsteel judgment is welcomed and further confirms the correct approach in law, that in instances where it is legally impermissible for employees to perform their duties, the employer is entitled to enforce the "no work, no pay" principle based on the impossibility of performance by both parties. The judgment affirmed the application of the "no work, no pay" principle, specifically that employees who were unable to work during the COVID-19 lockdown were not entitled to their salaries.

title: Interrogating the Practice of Lawful Interception of Communications and the Right to Privacy in Nigeria and South Africa
author: David T Eyongndi, Garvin U Oyibodoro, Onyinye Ucheagwu-Okoye, Ademola O Ojekunle, Chidimma S Nwakoby, Hilary Nwaechefu
summary: Section 37 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (CFRN 1999) guarantees the right to privacy. This right is recognised by international legal frameworks like the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966 and, by expansive interpretation, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, 1981. However, section 45 of the CFRN 1999 empowers the legislature to make laws that derogate from specific rights under Chapter IV thereof, and section 37 is one of the derogable rights. Consequently the Nigerian Communications Act, 2003 (NCA 2003), which established the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) with powers to make regulations, was enacted. Pursuant to the NCA 2003 the NCC made the Lawful Interception of Communications Regulations, 2019 (LICR 2019), permitting security agencies to intercept communications in furtherance of national security, crime prevention/investigation, safeguarding the economic well-being of Nigerians, etc. As in Nigeria, the right to privacy is guaranteed in South Africa, but the Regulation of Interception of Communications and Provision of Communication-Related Information Act 70 of 2002 (RICA 2002) permits the interception of communication, with reasonable guardrails provided. The issues arising from this practice are the following. Is the interception of communication under the LICR 2019 and RICA 2002 a necessity or an intrusion into the right of privacy? How can the right to privacy be safeguarded against this practice? And what lessons can Nigeria learn from the South African experience on the interception of communication? This article adopts a comparative method, relying on primary and secondary data in interrogating these issues, gleaning from the practice in South Africa. It finds that the implementation of the LICR 2019 is susceptible to abuse by the implementers, unlike the RICA 2002, which contains guardrails; that the sanctions prescribed for violation by implementers are incapable of instilling deterrence, and that there is a need to create a symbiotic co-existence between the right to privacy and the LICR 2019. It recommends the amendment of the LICR 2019 by the imposition of stiffer sanctions for breach, and the public enlightenment of security agencies towards lawful implementation.

title: Food Security as a Consideration in Anti-Dumping Investigations Conducted by the International Trade Administration Commission: Lessons for South Africa from the European Commission
author: Jeanette Visagie, Marucia Fick
summary: Following the decision by the South African Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition to suspend anti-dumping duties in the International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) Chicken Meat Dumping Investigation case, and the subsequent outbreak of disease amongst poultry, this article analyses the need to consider food security as part of the ‘public interest’ during anti-dumping investigations relating to essential food products. ITAC and the Minister of Trade are mandated, in terms of the relevant legal framework, to consider public interest as an additional fourth requirement on an ad hoc basis during anti-dumping investigations that may impact food security in South Africa and other Southern African Customs Union countries. Accessibility and availability elements of food security are affected by factors such as the type of product and whether it is an essential food, possible supply constraints impacting local food production, the prevalence or risk of disease outbreak, and the likelihood that price increases following the imposition of anti-dumping duties will be passed on to the end consumer. ITAC should consider these factors during anti-dumping investigations in a manner similar to the European Union’s consideration of the Union interest, ultimately assisting the Minister of Trade in making a decision regarding the imposition of anti-dumping duties in matters related to essential food products. If such an approach is adopted, it would be in line with the government’s obligation and responsibility to protect, promote and fulfil the right to access to sufficient food.

It is extensive in its coverage as it attempts to exhaust a large proportion of protections that are provided to indigenous knowledge specialities such as heritage protection, Africa's Scientific Technical Indigenous Knowledge (STIK) protections, indigenous designs, indigenous literary knowledge, sign terms and expressions and various cultural expressions in the African audiovisual industry and indigenous African music.

title: WTO Safeguards in Africa: Limited Use, Compliance Challenges and Capacity Constraints
author: Gustav Brink
summary: Safeguards are one of three World Trade Organization (WTO)-sanctioned trade remedies that countries may use to protect their domestic industries against various forms of increased international competition. However, few African countries make use of the instrument, with only Egypt, Madagascar, Morocco and South Africa as active users, while three more countries have each conducted a single safeguard investigation. There are some WTO inconsistencies in the way each of these countries conduct safeguard investigations, but nothing that cannot be addressed without too much effort. Other African countries, especially the more industrialised countries such as Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, should finalise their safeguards legislation and request technical assistance from the WTO and the African countries actively using the instrument to rapidly upskill to allow themselves to use the instrument. Safeguards can be instrumental in protecting domestic industries against increased imports and allow them the opportunity to adjust to such increased competition, thereby enabling African countries to participate more fully in international trade and beneficiate raw materials domestically, all of which could contribute to Africa’s economic growth.

title: Educational Standards, Qualifications and Competency Frameworks for Councillors in South African Municipalities—A Constitutional Need
author: Nonhlanhla Ngcobo
summary: The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (CoGTA) is currently reviewing the 1998 White Paper on Local Government, marking the beginning of a new era for a sphere whose constitutional and legislative powers have significantly contributed to the development of local communities. Despite this recognition, local government continues to face persistent challenges, including deficiencies in administrative governance, service delivery backlogs, infrastructure constraints, and both financial and structural limitations. However, the review of the White Paper fails to acknowledge that many of these challenges can be significantly attributed to the low literacy levels of councillors—the key decision-makers in municipalities—among other factors. This omission persists despite the minister’s public admission that more than 300 councillors in the KwaZulu-Natal Province are unable to read or write. This article argues that the absence of minimum educational, expertise and competency requirements for councillors may undermine the effective implementation of the proposed reforms, especially given the increasing complexity of political, financial and administrative tasks and decision-making within the local government sphere. The article undertakes a critical analysis of political rights and principles enshrined in the Constitution in the context of the dysfunctional local government in South Africa, and in response, offers a carefully crafted councillor competency capacity development framework that does not encroach on the relevant constitutional guarantees.

title: Eligibility of Victims of International Crimes for Reparations before the International Criminal Court: A Critique
author: Bongani M Dlamini, Linda Mushoriwa
summary: The adoption of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court on 17 July 1998 and the establishment of the International Criminal Court (ICC or the Court) on 2 July 2002 marked a significant turn for international criminal justice. Notably, the Court established a platform for bringing justice to victims of international crimes, whilst putting the victims at the centre of proceedings. One way in which this is evident is the framework for awarding reparations to victims of the core crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. This not only serves to acknowledge the victims’ pain and suffering but also to remedy the harm they have suffered. The Court’s mandate to award reparations to victims of international crimes is provided for in Article 75 of the Rome Statute. The purpose of this article is to examine the Court’s reparations regime with respect to the eligibility of victims to receive reparations as provided for in the Rome Statute, and as seen through the lens of the Court’s jurisprudence on this subject. The article asserts that whilst the reparations regime is an innovative way to deliver justice to victims of atrocities, its effectiveness remains subject to debate due to challenges associated with the interpretation of the meaning of ‘victims’ for purposes of reparations, and the eligibility criteria for victims to be awarded reparations. It concludes that the Court must consider amending its procedural laws to allow flexibility and place more prominence on the content of reparations delivered in individual cases.

title: Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation in Zimbabwe: Lessons from South Africa
author: Basutu S Makwaiba
summary: The purpose of this article is to critically review the judicial approach to delegated legislation in Zimbabwe. One of the firmly entrenched principles in constitutional law is that legislative power cannot be delegated. The limitation on the legislature’s delegation of its primary law-making powers is based on the doctrine of non-delegation. The non-delegation doctrine commands that the legislature alone exercise law-making power. This article examines the extent to which the Zimbabwean courts have enforced the non-delegation doctrine when reviewing executive law-making under the Presidential Powers (Temporary Measures) Act. The courts have held that the Act is constitutional even though it assigns Parliament’s primary law-making to the executive. The article used a doctrinal research methodology to analyse existing primary and secondary sources. It also included a desk review, which employed a comparative methodology. The comparative analysis focused on South Africa, selected for its judiciary’s ability to exert stronger oversight over the delegation of legislative authority to the executive. The South African courts have defined the limits to which legislative powers may be delegated distinguishing between delegation to make subordinate legislation and assigning primary law-making power to another body. This article aims to contribute to the existing literature on the nature and extent of constitutional limitations on the delegation of legislative powers. There is a conspicuous dearth of scholarly literature examining judicial oversight of delegated legislation in Zimbabwe, and this study addresses that gap.

title: Editorial: Legal-Technical Governance and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Africa
author: Chijioke Okorie, Vukosi Marivate
summary: This editorial introduces the special issue on the legal-technical governance and regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa, the product of a project launched by the Data Science Law Lab in collaboration with the Data Science for Social Impact research group at the University of Pretoria. It situates the five peer-reviewed contributions within a legal-technical approach to AI governance: a transdisciplinary approach in which the legal and the technical are fused to add nuance to regulatory forms and practices and to close the legal-technical gap in AI governance and regulation. The contributions move from conceptual foundations, where legal-technical governance is advanced as an analytical framework, through continental norm-making on the transition from African Union soft law to an AI treaty and national policy design on intellectual property in African AI strategies, to the operation of AI systems in practice, addressing the algorithmic sovereignty gap in AI-enabled surveillance in South Africa and Nigeria and the legal status of predictive policing in the fight against cybercrime in Nigeria.

title: ESTA Occupiers and the Construction of Buildings and Homesteads on Farmland: Addressing Critical Issues in Light of Prinsloo NO v Ngcongwane [2023] ZALCC 22 and Basfour 3327 (Pty) Ltd v Thwala (Leave to Appeal) [2023] ZALCC 28
author: Lerato Rudolph Ngwenyama
summary: The purpose of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act (62 of 1997) (ESTA) is to enhance and promote the ideal of long-term security of tenure for occupiers of land on an equitable basis, promote land-tenure reform as a means of redressing the results of past discrimination and facilitate land-tenure justice. The history of land dispossession and labour tenancy is important to this context and connects with the purpose of ESTA. To fulfil the purpose of ESTA as contemplated in the Preamble, the objects of ESTA are, among others, to afford certain rights and duties to persons who reside on land that they do not own.

title: Lawyers are Safe from the AI Invasion—For Now! A Brief Consideration of the Use of Artificially Generated Tools in Legal Research in SA and the US
author: Ciresh Singh, Menelisi Ncube
summary: A legal maxim holds that ‘it is not knowing all the law that counts but knowing where to find the law that makes a good lawyer a great lawyer,’ highlighting the importance of legal research. While technology and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed research and drafting, they are prone to errors, including fabricated authorities. Courts, especially in the United States (US), have sanctioned misuse and South African courts have raised concerns, though no regulations yet exist. This paper examines AI use in legal research by undertaking a detailed analysis of the recent case law, in the US and South Africa, that has considered this topic. This paper will be divided into five parts: Part 1 serves as an introduction and overview of the topic; Part 2 briefly considers some of the AI tools currently available and their possible application in legal practice; Part 3 investigates how some AI tools have been used in the US; Part 4 considers the use of AI tools in the South African legal system; and Part 5 serves as a conclusion and provides some key recommendations in this area. It is hoped that this discussion will bring to light the need for AI regulation and, possibly, the prompt implementation of guidelines and rules to regulate its use not only in legal practice, but also in society. The article draws on both primary and secondary materials and employs a qualitative desktop research method. This article calls for, inter alia, concerted efforts by the legislature and other relevant stakeholders to comprehensively regulate the use of AI by legal practitioners when conducting legal research in order to retain the integrity of the South African legal profession.

title: Integration of AI tools into management and governance of humanitarian projects in conflict-affected North-West Nigeria
author: Akaninyene O. Unaam, Etini A. Unaam
summary: <jats:p>Humanitarian projects in conflict zones face extreme complexity caused by, inter alia, volatility, fragmentation, and accountability pressures. Such complexity often renders conventional project implementation approaches inadequate. This study, focused on the conflict zone of North-West Nigeria, investigated the extent to which artificial intelligence (AI) tools can enhance the effectiveness of management governance and governance of humanitarian projects. Grounded in sociotechnical systems (STS) theory, the study surveyed 300 project personnel across Kebbi, Katsina, and Jigawa States, and conducted interviews with 25 of the personnel. Statistical analysis of the quantitative data from the survey found that the adoption of AI tools had a statistically significant correlation with project management effectiveness (β = .46, p < .001), with organisational readiness and ethical governance found to serve as significant partial mediators. The qualitative findings from the interview data identified AI tools’ positive roles in project management and governance—through support for (human-led) decision support, transparency, and anticipatory governance—but also revealed tensions around equity, attentional displacement, and the marginalisation of national actors.</jats:p>

title: Instability absorption by tertiary educators: Technology adoption under conditions of fragility in the Liberian higher education sector
author: Olajide Jolugbo, Agnes Reeves-Taylor
summary: <jats:p>Digital transformation in higher education is frequently framed in terms of access and adoption. Such framings generally failed to consider how digital higher education systems function under conditions of persistent infrastructural instability and constrained institutional capacity. This study examines Liberian educators’ experiences of digital provision under conditions of fragility in the country’s higher education sector. Based on data from interviews and a survey with 22 educators across 11 Liberian tertiary institutions, the research found that continuity is sustained to a great extent not through the provision of technological systems and user acceptance of those systems, but rather through educators’ adaptations to the unstable state of the technological infrastructure. The educators’ responses fall into four main instability absorption categories—responsibility displacement; non-institutional and informal communication infrastructures; communicative labour; and uneven digital labour—and the study proposes the instability absorption model (IAM) to explain how these absorption practices sustain digital education delivery. The model frames technology adoption under conditions of fragility as a process of sustained operationalisation, where systems continue functioning through continuous human absorption of infrastructure disruption.</jats:p>

title: Bridging global and local influences: Kenya’s emerging approach to AI governance
author: Jeremiah Osida Onunga
summary: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified demand for national AI governance frameworks that balance innovation with ethical, legal, and societal safeguards. Emerging economies such as Kenya face the dual challenge of seeking to foster AI-driven growth while at the same time managing numerous risks. This study explores Kenya’s emerging approach to AI governance, as represented by its Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030 and Artificial Intelligence Bill of 2026. Through policy–legislative content analysis, the study examines the degree to which Kenya’s approach is both transplanting and localising the orientation and provisions of the EU’s influential AI governance instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024. The research also applies a contextual-adaptation analysis to examine the extent to which Kenya’s AI governance approach is geared towards its particular national needs.</jats:p>

title: Negotiating and navigating colourism in Cuba and Ghana: Perspectives represented in the work of Cuban poet Nicolás Guillén and in Ghanaian TikTok and YouTube content
author: Franklina Kabio-Danlebo, Setor Donne Novieto
summary: <jats:p>There is a strong body of literature on colourism—discrimination among people of colour on the basis of darkness or lightness of skin tone—as it has manifested, and continues to manifest, among Black communities in the Americas and Africa. The phenomenon, with its roots in colonialism, is sufficiently powerful to produce a wide range of social, cultural, and economic effects and a wide range of responses, including skin-bleaching practices that can have severe health consequences. This study explores the dynamics of colourism in two national contexts, Cuba and Ghana, which are highly distinct from each other and at the same time both strongly marked by the sociocultural legacies of colonialism, including the phenomenon of colourism. The study examines Cuban colourism as it is explored and combatted in the 1930s poetry of Cuban writer Nicolás Guillén, and Ghanaian colourism as it is both promoted and critiqued in contemporary TikTok and YouTube social-media content.</jats:p>

title: Digital public infrastructure (DPI) across Africa: A national identity systems perspective
author: Jonathan Klaaren
summary: <jats:p>A rising global politics advocates for national investments in digital public infrastructure (DPI). The national DPI paradigm combines three core elements: digital national identity systems, digital national payment systems, and safe and secure data exchange. This study, grounded in literature on national identity systems and legal identity, assesses digital national identity systems in several African countries. Based on two of the core functions of identity systems (identification, authentication), as well as identity systems’ linkages to national payments systems, the study conceptualises four main types of digital national identity systems present in African countries: identification-led, authentication-led, plural, and payments-led. The study tests the applicability of the typology on a set of 11 African jurisdictions and finds that eight of the jurisdictions fit within the typology: South Africa, Uganda and Zambia (identification-led systems); Ethiopia and Morocco (authentication-led systems); Ghana (plural system); and Kenya and Nigeria (payments-led systems). The study contributes to global DPI debates by emphasising the authentication function in identity systems, by problematising the relationship between national identity systems and payment systems, and by engaging with global DPI indicators.</jats:p>

title: SCA Provides Clarity on the Requirements Needed for the Court to Grant Remedial Action for Oppressive and Unfair Conduct in Terms of Section 163 of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 - Parry v Dunn-Blatch [2024] ZASCA 19
author: Darren Subramanien, Dehal Jivan, Suhail Ebrahim
summary: The “oppression remedy”, while having arguably undergone substantial legislative development over time, has long been a contentious issue for South African courts. The use of this remedy allows shareholders or directors to challenge, and seek relief from, certain acts or omissions they believe are oppressive or unfairly prejudicial, or that unfairly disregard their interests. In Parry v Dunn-Blatch ([2024] ZASCA 19), the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) had to consider whether the act or omission envisaged in section 163(1) of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 (the 2008 Act) had taken place as alleged by the applicant. The decision of the SCA in Parry v Dunn-Blatch (supra) is important as the court provided much-needed clarity as to what will be required by an applicant who wishes to bring a successful application for use of the remedy found in section 163 of the 2008 Act.

title: Competition Law as a Catalyst for Access to Education: A Review of a Drive against Anti-Competitive Practices in the Procurement of School Uniforms by the Competition Commission of South Africa
author: Sandiso Mbulawa
summary: Exclusive agreements and high prices in some markets can harm competition, competitors, and consumers and may also affect the enjoyment of constitutionally protected rights. Some practices impinge on aspects of citizens’ fundamental rights, such as the right of access to education. In response to complaints from parents regarding anti-competitive practices involving schools, suppliers and/or manufacturers, the Competition Commission has undertaken a series of interventions to enhance competition in the procurement of school uniforms and other related materials. The initiative was aimed at promoting and balancing increasing competition in school-uniform procurement and to provide parents with more choices to ensure that they are not compelled to purchase school uniforms exclusively from selected suppliers. The initiative not only achieved market competitiveness, but, to a certain extent, it also secured the constitutional right to access to education. Therefore, the article examines the effectiveness of the Competition Commission’s interventions on the procurement of school uniforms and showcases the role the agency played in promoting access to education.

title: Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 3)
author: Jan-Louis van Tonder
summary: Sections 4(1)(a) and (b) of the Competition Act 89 of 1998 reflect the distinction in competition law between horizontal restrictive practices that may be evaluated either through a “rule of reason” analysis or treated as automatically unlawful under a “per se” approach. Section 4(1)(a) contemplates a “rule of reason” analysis in terms of which the anti-competitive effects of the conduct in issue must be proved and, even if such effects are demonstrated, they are susceptible to justification on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. By contrast, where the impugned conduct involves any of the restrictive horizontal practices listed in section 4(1)(b), namely, price-fixing, market division or collusive tendering, it is prohibited “per se” in that the anti-competitive effect thereof is presumed and cannot be justified on technological, efficiency or pro-competitive grounds. As is the case with bona fide agreements that are embarked upon by competitors for a legitimate purpose, commercially reasonable ancillary restraints, even when concluded between competitors, ought not to be treated as automatically infringing section 4(1)(b) without further enquiry. For these purposes, the Competition Appeal Court (CAC) in Dawn Consolidated Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission (Dawn) has developed a well-refined test to assess whether a restraint of trade within a broader agreement, such as a joint venture, falls within the scope of the prohibitions enacted by section 4(1)(b) of the Competition Act. Part 1 critically reviews the applicable South African framework and principles relevant to characterisation as developed in American Natural Soda Ash Corporation v Competition Commission and Competition Commission v South African Breweries Ltd and assesses the approach to whether conduct is anti-competitive by object or effect under article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (EU). Part 2 builds on Part 1 by reviewing and assessing key facets of characterisation that have further emerged from notable cases such as Aranda Textile Mills (Pty) Ltd v The Competition Commission of South Africa, Tourvest Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission, Competition Commission of South Africa v Irwin & Johnson, and Competition Commission v Waco Africa (Pty) Ltd. Part 3 reviews and assesses the approach relevant to characterisation of ancillary restraints of trade as developed by the CAC in Dawn. Pursuant to section 1(3) of the Competition Act, appropriate foreign and international law may be considered when interpreting or applying the Competition Act. This is complementary to section 1(2)(a), which directs that the Competition Act must be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the Constitution and that gives effect to the purposes set out in section 2. In light hereof, this article also considers the approaches in the United Kingdom, the EU and the United States. (Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 1)” 2025 46(4) Obiter 872–886; Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 2)” 2026 47(1) Obiter 1–14)

title: Foreclosure of Primary Home Mortgages in Namibia: Towards Efficient Judicial Oversight
author: PC Nhekairo, NV Asheela-Shikalepo
summary: Mortgage foreclosures represent a significant and contentious issue, particularly when they pertain to individuals’ primary homes. Foreclosure inherently creates a conflict between two opposing interests: the mortgagee’s entitlement to enforce their security and the imperative to alleviate the severe repercussions of displacing the mortgagor and their family, which could lead to homelessness. In Namibia, the relevance of mortgage foreclosure concerning primary homes is exacerbated by a persistent housing crisis; thus, displacing a mortgagor and their family contributes to the alarming statistic that about 25 per cent of the population lacks access to adequate housing. The interplay of interests among the mortgagor, the mortgagee and external entities such as the government necessitates a careful balancing exercise in the enforcement of mortgage foreclosures. The execution of foreclosures on primary homes in Namibia is primarily governed by rule 108 of the High Court Rules, which mandates judicial oversight prior to declaring primary homes specially executable. This article contends that the existing regulatory framework in Namibia does not adequately reconcile the competing interests associated with the foreclosure of primary homes. Based on the results of a comparative analysis, this article ultimately proposes the promulgation of a comprehensive foreclosure regulatory framework.

title: The Constitutional and Legislative Powers of Local Authorities in South Africa: The Applicability of an Ocean Accounts Framework as an Ocean-Governance Instrument
author: Hendrik J Van As
summary:
This research examines the Ocean Accounts Framework (OAF) as an instrument for ocean governance and policy development by South African local authorities. The Constitution imposes sustainable developmental duties on municipalities, requiring them to budget and plan in a way that prioritises basic community needs and promotes social and economic development. With their funding primarily coming from property rates, service surcharges and payments from national government, municipalities are responsible for local economic and infrastructure development, promoting a safe and healthy environment, and service delivery.

Coastal management is the shared responsibility of all three branches of government and frequently overlaps. South Africa adopted the National Development Plan (NDP) to promote economic growth and address the triple challenge of inequality, unemployment and poverty. Operation Phakisa prioritises marine transport, offshore oil and gas, aquaculture and marine protection services. 

This article examines the relationship between the OAF and the legislative and policy instruments that guide coastal and ocean governance in South Africa’s local government sphere. As part of a community of practice (CoP), the research assesses the applicability of the OAF in South Africa and the Western Indian Ocean (WIO), with a focus on the legal context in which the OAF is to be used. It investigates the constitutional and legislative powers and functions of local authorities that are relevant to the blue economy and the extent to which municipalities exercise these powers and functions. It also assesses the OAF’s potential to evaluate food security and sustainability risks for local populations, and whether local authorities can legislate against marine-resource crimes to augment national legislation. Finally, the study argues that using the OAF to measure ocean value for municipal development could boost funding and help local authorities meet the requirements set by the Constitution, the NDP and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Local authorities should realise the importance of the ocean and its living resources and use a credible valuation tool to exercise their legislative powers.

title: Unconstitutional Transitions or Constitutions without Constitutionalism in Africa? A Review of Cameroon and Gabon Experiences
author: Elisabeth Achancho Etagha
summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>African constitutional practice continues to grapple with challenges of political instability and contested legitimacy. This article critically examines the tension between unconstitutional transitions and constitutions without constitutionalism in Africa, with a particular focus on the experiences of Cameroon and Gabon. It explores how formal constitutional frameworks, while outwardly adhering to legal norms, have been systematically manipulated to entrench authoritarian rule and undermine democratic legitimacy. Drawing on constitutional texts, legal reforms, and political events from both countries, the article distinguishes between de facto unconstitutional changes of government and de jure constitutional orders that nonetheless contravene fundamental democratic principles. The analysis employs a comparative constitutional methodology, supplemented by political theory and historical context, to evaluate the extent to which constitutions in these cases serve as instruments of democratic governance or authoritarian consolidation. The research reveals that in both cases, constitutional frameworks have been strategically modified to legitimise authoritarian rule, blurring the line between legality and illegitimacy. It calls for a reconceptualisation of constitutional practice in Africa, one that moves beyond formal legality toward substantive democratic norms rooted in accountability, participation, and human rights.</jats:p>

title: The House of Representatives of Zanzibar’s Encroachment on Union Constitutional Legislative Powers in Tanzania
author: Ryoba Marwa
summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This Article examines the constitutional legal framework governing the division of legislative powers between the Union Parliament and the House of Representatives of Zanzibar within the United Republic of Tanzania. The United Republic of Tanzania operates under a unique constitutional arrangement that combines elements of both federalism and unitary governance. The study employed doctrinal analysis to examine how the House of Representatives of Zanzibar has encroached upon the Union Parliament’s legislative powers, thereby contravening the supremacy of the Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania. This study revealed that the House of Representatives of Zanzibar has consistently exceeded its legislative powers, despite constitutional limits, by passing laws on ports, maritime exclusive economic zones, and petroleum resources, all of which are classified as Union Matters. This creates legal uncertainty, administrative duplication, enforcement fragmentation and jeopardises the integrity of the Union. The study concludes that these legislative intrusions contravene the principle of constitutional supremacy and recommends constitutional reform to strengthen safeguards against jurisdictional overlap and to align enacted laws with the Union’s constitutional supremacy.</jats:p>

title: Comparative analysis of child consent laws in health care decisions in South Africa, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada
author: Frans Mahlobogwane
summary: Over the last few decades, laws worldwide have increasingly evolved to allow minors to, inter alia, consent to their own health care services. These laws, when compared, are oftentimes inconsistent with one another, with variations between countries as regards the minimum age of consent, the classes of minors that may consent, and the context within which consent may be considered valid. Furthermore, these laws have altered the discourse on health care access as it relates to children, specifically because health care providers must adhere to minor consent laws when addressing the needs of adolescent patients. Considering the above it is crucial, in a comparative and medico legal context, to understand whether and how minors may consent on their own to receive various types of health care services. This paper reflects on the way in which various jurisdictions, including South Africa, have treated the issue of child consent when it comes to health care decisions and services. It provides a brief overview of the laws governing minors’ capacity to consent to health care, considering the complexity of the concept of evolving legal standing and the process of children’s participation in the health care environment. Comparing South Africa with the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada reveals distinct legal philosophies, specifically the shift from fixed-age limits to “competence-based” assessments. Consequently, the paper recommends that South Africa would do well to develop guiding principles for assessing a child’s decision-making capacity in line with international practices.

title: Contra non valentem in South Africa: A transformative evaluation of whether the death of a land owner should delay the completion of acquisitive prescription∗
author: Ernst Marais
summary: The Gauteng Local Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, recently had to decide a vexing legal question, namely whether the law delays (or postpones) the running of acquisitive prescription (“prescription”) under the contra non valentem agere non currit praescriptio (prescription does not run against those who cannot assert their rights) maxim if a landowner passed away. If so, prescription would be postponed until the beneficiaries appointed an executor to the deceased estate. The court answered this question affirmatively by holding that no one can stop (or interrupt) the running of prescription prior to the appointment of an executor, that prescription promotes legal certainty and not the personal interest of the possessor, and that the possessor’s acquiring ownership in a case like the present could possibly entail an arbitrary deprivation of the deceased owner’s property. This paper investigates the legal question from the perspective of South African private law doctrine, comparative law, legal theory, and in terms of the property and housing clauses in the Constitution. My conclusions are that (i) beneficiaries have standing to interrupt prescription, (ii) foreign law favours the promotion of legal certainty over the protection of an (incapacitated) owner when the prescription period is long, (iii) postponing prescription in a case like Katha v Pillay discourages beneficiaries from appointing an executor timeously, thereby causing further neglect of the land (and prolonging the uncertainty of its legal status), (iv) recognising too many grounds of postponement would undermine the legal certainty rationale in countries with negative registration systems (like South Africa), (v) moral reasons indicate that a possessor’s long-existing home interest in land is worthy of protection, and (vi) that vesting ownership of land in such a possessor would amount to a transformative outcome, despite the owner’s death (provided she satisfies the other prescription requirements as well). These conclusions draw the court’s ruling on the postponement matter into question.

title: Piercing the trust veil at divorce: A constitutionally compliant common law approach to rendering trust assets liable to attachment in satisfaction of matrimonial property claims – Part One
author: Bradley Smith
summary: Remedial action following a court’s decision to “pierce the veil” of an abused trust at divorce typically involves adding a trust’s asset value for the purposes of calculating the errant spouse’s matrimonial property liability. Although the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) has mooted the possibility of further action via a declaration that trust assets are to be “used … to satisfy” a patrimonial claim, this avenue remains unexplored. It has, however, recently come to light that in the 2020 matter of LW v CW, the Western Cape High Court ordered the transfer of an abused trust’s assets “[i]n the event of [the errant spouse] holding insufficient assets in his personal capacity to satisfy [the other spouse’s] accrual claim.” This notwithstanding, in 2023 the South African Law Reform Commission (SALRC) proposed an amendment to the Divorce Act 70 of 1979 that would empower a court to distribute trust property to a spouse whose matrimonial property entitlement has been frustrated by means of a trust. Part One of this contribution argues that while the ability to access trust assets by judicial intervention is essential to affording effective relief to such spouses, statutory reform is unnecessary. This is because the common law provides a viable alternative, by instead permitting trust assets to be attached, if necessary, to satisfy a matrimonial property debt. This assertion is based on answering what this contribution identifies as the core “deprivation question”, namely whether the common law principles pertaining to piercing the corporate veil permit a company to be deprived of its assets to satisfy a debt that is not its own, but rather that of a related individual (such as a shareholder) owed to a third party. An analysis of pre-constitutional case law – as the only available case law on point – permits the distillation of several fundamental precepts that permit a positive answer to this question. The discussion then moves to the trust/divorce law context, where the principles which have become established – as well as those that can be deduced – from leading SCA case law in respect of a court’s ability to pierce the veil of an abused trust at divorce and their potential relevance to the deprivation question are considered. Building on these, Part One concludes with preliminary insights into the theoretical underpinnings of rendering trust property liable to attachment at divorce. Part Two will expand on these underpinnings by considering the constitutional ramifications of the deprivation question. Ultimately, this comprehensive analysis will achieve the main aim of this contribution, which is to conceptualise a constitutionally compliant approach to be followed by aggrieved spouses who seek the potential attachment of trust assets where necessary. To this end, an incremental development of the common law is required. Part Two will conclude by comparing this approach to the one taken in LW v CW with a view to securing a more satisfactory legal position.

title: The coordinated role and functions of international finance institutes in mitigating economic crime and fostering financial stability: A multi-dimensional South African analysis
author: Eureka Eulogy Ndhlovu
summary: Within South Africa’s evolving financial regulatory landscape, global financial institutions play an increasingly critical role in shaping anti-economic crime strategies and fostering financial stability. This paper undertakes a multi-dimensional analysis of the coordinated and individual contributions of the Institute of International Finance (IIF), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the World Economic Forum (WEF), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank (WB), the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) in mitigating economic crime. While the discussion draws on global policy frameworks and innovation models, it remains rooted in the South African context , examining national legal instruments, regulatory sandboxes, and fintech developments. Case studies from South Africa and peer jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, Nigeria, and Singapore offer comparative insight into sandbox mechanisms. Ultimately, the paper evaluates how international institutions influence domestic frameworks and provides South Africa-focused recommendations for regulatory enhancement.

title: Inferior by law –Ethnographic results in the Limpopo province of the interaction between traditional justice and the state law as encompassed by the Traditional Courts Act
author: Lesetja Monyamane
summary: South African jurisprudence attempts to employ a dual trajectory of law that includes customary law. However, this duality has been – and regrettably remains – faulty in that it has never properly accounted for the perversion caused to the system of customary law by the now repealed Black Administration Act 38 of 1927. Despite being repealed, its disregard of Native legal imagination and the cultural location of customary law remain largely unaccounted for in South Africa. The paper finds it edifying that this disregard of Native legal capital and imagination has been furthered by the provisions of the Traditional Courts Act 9 of 2022. It is the further contention of the author that the Traditional Courts Act attempts to project traditional justice as an unsophisticated form of justice which is inferior to the state law and its other justice operatives. It is argued below that the Act perpetuates and sustains this supposed inferiority of customary law by intentionally excluding the true legal imagination and experiences of the Natives in determining their legal issues. The paper furthermore interrogates this marginalisation through an ethnographic inquiry conducted in the Limpopo Province, South Africa. The ethnographic data demonstrates a rich tapestry of traditional justice that is not only responsive but is indeed multifaceted. In essence, it is argued here, the Traditional Courts Act is a new attempt underlying the insistence by the state law to undermine customary law and, by extension, traditional justice.

title: Transformation through the lens of South Africa’s Competition Act 89 of 1998
author: Tinashe Kondo
summary: In this paper, I examine how and whether transformation can be achieved through South Africa’s Competition Act 89 of 1998. This issue is important due to the lack of studies exploring the linkages between transformation and competition law, particularly after the enactment of the Competition Amendment Act 18 of 2018. The inclusion of transformation objectives in the Competition Act 89 of 1998 (the Act/ Competition Act), as amended, has been a subject of debate, with some arguing that the primary goal of competition law should be economic efficiency and that transformation goals may conflict with this mandate. However, I contend that there is a theoretical foundation for incorporating transformation issues into the Competition Act 89 of 1998, supported by both economic and legal theory. I observe that transformation is a policy demand arising from South Africa’s competition policy. The paper furthermore explores how transformation has been integrated into the Act, illustrating that it is no longer merely an aspiration in competition law but is now embedded in various provisions beyond merger regulation and the Act’s stated purpose. Consequently, transformation has become a key consideration in the Act’s implementation and enforcement. My main argument in the paper is that transformation is not merely an economic consideration, but a legal imperative rooted in South Africa’s constitutional values and historical injustices. I recommend that legislators explore ways to better promote other transformation goals such as: advancing employment and improving the social and economic welfare of South Africa within the framework of the Act; considering ways to concretise the centrality of constitutional and human rights objectives within the Act; and including constitutional values as interpretive aids in the Act. In relation to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and businesses owned by historically disadvantaged persons (HDPs), I make the case that there be ways developed to quantify the harm to them as well as monitor the digital markets more closely for harm to these entities. Finally, I encourage competition authorities to examine the possible role and impact of other principles and values, such as ubuntu, within competition law.

title: Challenging property law's faceless "reason" through literature and language
author: Dr Tanveer R. Jeewa
summary: Property law has long relied on its lack of empathy to remain the most loyal servant of capitalism — a discipline shaped by the pursuit of stability, predictability, and the protection of capital. Seeking to present itself as a law of reason, it reflects the logic of a market that demands abstraction over humanity and order over justice. Under Classical Legal Thought, property law’s legal subject became faceless and contextless, a construct designed to serve economic rationality rather than human experience. Yet, in South Africa’s constitutional era, this detachment has been challenged through the emergence of literature as a tool of legal reasoning. This article explores how literature disrupts property law’s formalism by reintroducing empathy, history, and humanity into judicial decision-making. Through an analysis of Constitutional Court judgments, I examine three categories of property law decisions: those that engage with literature and recognise unequal power relations; those that do not rely on literature where parties stand on more equal footing; and those that, despite stark inequalities, remain devoid of literary or empathetic engagement. These case studies demonstrate literature’s ability to pierce through property law’s rational veneer, compelling judges to confront the lived experiences of those before them. By contrasting the formalist rigidity of Classical Legal Thought with the transformative potential of literature, I argue that literature’s narrative and justificatory functions allow for a more humane application of the law, one that allows property law to move beyond its illusion of neutrality — towards empathy, contextual sensitivity, and an engagement with the stories that constitute the human condition.

title: Abezimu/Badimo (ancestors) and copyright law: a decolonial exploration of the literary exception
author: Dr Ntando Sindane
summary: Heeding to the call to decolonise higher education and the law, in this article, I embrace a decolonial lens to grapple with copyright law in South Africa, and specifically the subject of authorship. The central claim is that Abezimu/Badimo (ancestors) are an author in a decolonised notion of copyright law. Whilst this claim is supported by scholarly interventions, as regards the essence of a pluriversal author, the objective is to substantively authenticate the central claim by drawing from contemporary African literature. Specifically, the article engages two of Mphuthumi Ntabeni’s works, these are his debut novel, Broken River Tent, and as well as his subsequent novel, The Wanderers. As part of this authenticating exercise, I contend with Johan van der Walt’s insights in relation to what he calls “the literary exception”. The latter proffers an incisive critique of some approaches in the field of law and literature. I figure that van der Walt requires some engagement, especially if one is to succeed in relying on African literature to authenticate/qualify the central claim that Abezimu/Badimo (ancestors) are an author in a decolonial understanding of copyright law.

title: Bifurcated worlds and copyright norms: a literary reflection on inclusive copyright, normative pluralism and the spectre of anarchy
author: Dr Richard Shay
summary: This article draws on AJ van der Walt’s insights into the legal transformation of society regarding the property law norms inherited at the dawn of constitutional democracy, and proceeds to develop and apply them in the context of contemporary South African copyright law. Specifically, this article reflects on the state of copyright law in South Africa by undertaking a literary analysis of two novels, namely, Kingsley Amis’s You can’t do both and Zakes Mda’s The Madonna of Excelsior. The novels are introduced as glimpses into two very different societies around the same time in history that are both governed by the same proprietary copyright norms. The roles of copyright works in the cultural and knowledge hierarchies within each society are explored, as well as how the characters in the respective novels engage with various forms of art, music and literature. Reflecting on Van der Walt’s utilisation of Amis’s novel to frame the tension between the purported stability anchored in social fundamentalism and the allure of change (and the spectre of anarchy that change presents to some) evident in a spate of Constitutional Court decisions during its 2007 term, this article outlines the same tension in the contemporary popular media rhetoric around the reform of copyright law. The portrayal of post-war England morality in Amis’s semi-autobiographical novel is contrasted to the Apartheid-era South African society depicted in Mda’s work, in which the white population of 1970s South Africa viewed normative pluralism as represented by the inclusion of black people’s interests – the very recognition of their dignity – with profound distrust, as such empowerment posed a direct threat to the socio-economic and political power they enjoyed in the country. This same fear of normative pluralism encroaching upon the entrenched power relations under the contemporary status quo is evident in the apologist rhetoric published in popular media that decries all attempts at copyright reform as simultaneously ignorant, malicious and corrupt. In this regard, the narrative styles of each novel are shown to be an apt illustration of moral agency as reflected in the competing exclusionary (self-interested) and inclusionary (other-regarding) approaches to copyright’s bedrock ideology and operative norms. Finally, the article considers the themes of sex and property as encountered in each novel as proxies for power over others and a means of enforcing normative modalities of self-interest against others, and the implications of the respective copyright norms for the broader political community and individuals’ place in their society are contemplated.

title: Figurations of the Australian carceral imaginary: the child, the paedophile and the cop
author: Prof. H van Rijswijk
summary: This article examines the figures of the child, the paedophile, and the cop in the Australian carceral imaginary, focusing on their deployment in legal and cultural narratives to justify state intervention and colonial control over First Nations communities. Through an analysis of Alexis Wright’s Plains of Promise (1997), Carpentaria(2006), The Swan Book (2013), and Praiseworthy (2023), the article argues that these figures function as central agents of colonial governance, sustaining state authority through legal fictions of protection and security. Wright’s novels systematically dismantle these mythologies, exposing how settler law constructs First Nations children as vulnerable subjects in need of state intervention, while simultaneously criminalizing First Nations men as threats. The figure of the paedophile, particularly as mobilized during the Northern Territory Intervention, serves as a racialized spectre that legitimates carceral expansion, while the cop operates as a violent enforcer of settler law, suppressing First Nations resistance. Wright’s fiction challenges these colonial representations by centring First Nations epistemologies, storytelling, and law as counter-narratives to state violence. The article situates Wright’s literary interventions within broader socio-legal debates on First Nations sovereignty, the Stolen Generations, and the failures of contemporary child protection policies. By reconfiguring the carceral figures of the child, the paedophile, and the cop, Wright’s work asserts an alternative jurisprudence—one that refuses the legitimacy of settler law and insists on the endurance of First Nations legal authority. The article concludes by considering the implications of Wright’s novels for a decolonial legal framework that transcends the limitations of the settler state.

title: Understanding law and literature through Freud's compromise formation
author: Prof. Angela Condello, Prof. Tiziano Toracca
summary: This article develops a theoretical framework that reconsiders the intersection between law and literature through the psychoanalytic notion of "compromise formation". We propose that both law and literature function as arts of compromise, mediating conflicts that are not only social or institutional, but also psychic and structural. Drawing on literary theory (notably Francesco Orlando’s reinterpretation of Freudian categories) and legal philosophy, the paper argues that both disciplines address ambivalence and contradiction, albeit differently: literature preserves and stages contradiction through figurality, while law resolves conflict through argumentation and decision-making. Three levels of compromise in law are outlined: foundational (the "contractual" basis of civilisation), ontological (legal object construction), and argumentative (interpretation and adjudication). We believe that using the literary model of compromise formation in legal reasoning and argumentation could offer new insights into how the law might handle deep moral and interpretive disagreements—particularly in areas like bioethics or civil rights—without necessarily suppressing contradiction. In doing so, the paper invites a paradigm shift in how we conceive of justice, interpretation, and legitimacy within the legal order.

title: Law, poetry and lack in Kandinsky, Rothko and Kentridge
author: Prof. Jaco Barnard-Naudé
summary: Following the work of Maria Aristodemou, while subtly departing from it, the article proposes a (novel) understanding of the relationship between law and “poetry” (instead of the more familiar “literature”) in the terms of the literary devices of metaphor and metonymy. I propose as the operative inoperative metaphor and metonymy at stake for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between law and poetry, the relationship between the Lacanian analyst and their analysand (in which lack is the central analytic category). From this vantage point, I investigate the visual poetry of three artists – Wassily Kandinsky, Mark Rothko and William Kentridge – who all had one or the other highly specific formative encounter with the law and, so the argument goes, went on transgressively to articulate that encounter with law in (at least some of) their poetry. I contend that each of these artists do not stop at the mere exposure of the lack in law that their poetry exposes, but are, rather also at pains to both proceed from and state the lack in poetry itself, thereby pointing up the existential lack of every subjective constitution. The analysis yields a critical divergence of law and literature, a necessary separation which nonetheless relates intimately, or extimately, in the form of the function of an analytics of law that leaves it in, or brings it to, a state of subjective destitution in which it may at last be able truly to apprehend for itself, the lack that makes it what it is.

title: The Routledge Handbook of Cultural Legal Studies
author: Isolde de Villiers
